juju · Operations · Self-monitoring

juju reports its own failures to a second juju

juju tells other people when their apps break. Until now nothing told us when juju broke: a failing query only left a line in a log file nobody was reading. Now the server sends its own errors and health to a second juju instance, and an outside check covers the case where the whole machine is gone.

[self-monitoring] VERIFIED LOCALLY outage="main Postgres stopped: monitor stayed up and raised platform.queue_backlog at 1200 events; 1201 of 1201 customer events stored after recovery; 0 customer text on the monitor"
The problem

A monitor can't report its own death

The obvious plan is to point juju's SDK at juju. It fails exactly when you need it: if the server is down, the thing that would send the alert is down too. A second instance helps with bugs and slow failures, but it runs on the same machine here to keep costs down, so it dies with the machine as well. That's why there are two layers, and each one covers what the other can't.

Hetzner server, myjuju.dev
juju.service :8080Customers' events. Sets JUJU_MONITOR_DSN.
juju-monitor.service :8081monitor.myjuju.dev. Its own user, queue and limits.
:8080 → :8081 errors, panics, backlogs, heartbeat. Counts and failure messages, never event contents.
Postgres and ClickHouse, sharedOne server each, with a separate database per instance. If Postgres stops, both instances lose their database.
Outside
Uptime checkSentry or similar, calling /readyz from elsewhere. Works when the whole server is gone.

How it works

Monitoring must never hurt the thing it monitors

Every choice below follows from that rule. A monitoring feature that can slow or stop production makes production less reliable, which is the opposite of the point.

Hooked into the logger

The server already logs each failure it handles. Wrapping the log handler reports every Error line, including ones in code not written yet, with no reporting call to remember at each failure point.

Capture never waits

Reporting happens on request paths, so it only drops an event into a buffer. A background loop does the network call. When the buffer is full, events are dropped and counted.

A storm has a ceiling

One batch of 50 every 5 seconds caps sending at 10 events a second. The instances share a machine, so an error storm on one must not become load on both.

No loop on failure

A failed send goes only to the local log. If it were reported as well, an unreachable monitor would make the server report on its own reporting forever.

A typo can't stop the server

A bad JUJU_MONITOR_DSN logs an error and turns reporting off. A DSN pointing at this same server is refused for the same reason it's useless.

Only what's needed leaves

Reports carry the log message, the error and the stack. Other log attributes stay behind, and panics send the route pattern, not the URL. Error text can still include details from the failure, and the monitor scrubs emails and tokens from it at ingest.

Thresholds raise issues instead of drawing a line chart because juju's analytics count events; they can't add up or average a number yet. Raising an issue reuses the alerts you already configure on a project, so this needed no new alerting code.

Using it

Turning it on

Merging ships the code but changes nothing on its own, because deploy.sh release doesn't run setup and JUJU_MONITOR_DSN starts empty.

# 1. DNS: point monitor.myjuju.dev at the server, then from your laptop:
deploy/deploy.sh setup root@2.31.22.112 myjuju.dev

# 2. On the server: make an account and a project on the monitor
juju-monitor-admin user create -email you@example.com -org platform
juju-monitor-admin project create -org platform -name juju

# 3. Copy the project's DSN from monitor.myjuju.dev into /etc/juju/juju.env.
#    Only the main instance gets this line, never monitor.env.
JUJU_MONITOR_DSN=https://pk_...@monitor.myjuju.dev/1
systemctl restart juju

# 4. In the uptime service: check https://myjuju.dev/readyz, expect 200

Setup also upgrades the server's packages and restarts services, so run it at a quiet time. Check free memory and disk first: this adds a second juju process to a small server.

Verification

What was checked

Two real juju processes on one laptop, each with its own Postgres, sharing one ClickHouse with two databases, as production will. Then main's Postgres was stopped.

Healthy server sends a heartbeat, raises no issuesjuju_monitor.events: platform.heartbeat, release juju@c1c64b19cd25, queue_pending 0. Issues on monitor: []

One bug turned up while testing: the stack filter skipped every function in the selfmon package, so the top frame in a test read testing.tRunner instead of the code that logged. It now skips only the reporter's own types.

Limits

What this doesn't cover yet

  • Not run on a real server. setup.sh, juju-receive and the systemd unit have only been syntax-checked, and the server's free memory and disk haven't been measured.
  • The alert itself wasn't sent. The runs stop at the issue appearing on the monitor. Sending to Slack or email is the existing alert path, and hasn't been run against these issues.
  • Worker crashes. A panic outside an HTTP request stops the process. systemd restarts it and the uptime check may catch the gap, but no report is sent.
  • Reporting delay in a database outage. Workers retry quietly, so the first sign can be the backlog alert or the uptime check, not an instant error.
  • Lost reports. Sends aren't retried, so a report sent while the monitor restarts is gone.
  • ClickHouse separation. Both instances use its default user, so the two databases prevent mix-ups but wouldn't stop a compromised instance.
  • Still to build. Per-organization and per-project usage history, on top of the super admin numbers, and JavaScript errors from the dashboard.
